reviews.text: This is a story of true love – a love between a husband and wife that only grew stronger through the many years they experienced together. It’s a love that’s taken for granted today and often times treated so flippantly.
reviews.author: Keith Garlington

reviews.text: In typical Haneke fashion, it leaves us with a deluge of questions about aging, dying, grief, and of course, love, but never dares to give an answer to any of them.
reviews.author: Eve O'Dea

reviews.text: Haneke's most resonant film considers that love has more dimension than we might believe, just as life alternates between harmonious times and inevitable conclusions.
reviews.author: Brian Eggert

reviews.text: Getting old is an ugly business and seldom a subject for cinema. I can't think of anyone more fitting than Michael Haneke to tackle this uncinematic, almost taboo subject.
reviews.author: Dustin Chang

reviews.text: Veteran Austrian auteur Michael Haneke eschews his trademark polarizing story tropes to produce a moving and complex portrait of the final months of a marriage between two retired Parisian music-teachers.
reviews.author: David Lamble

reviews.text: What makes Amour not only bearable but cathartic is the beauty of the filmmaking and the delicacy of the performances.
reviews.author: Amy Taubin

reviews.text: If love truly does overcome all things, then this is its ultimate test, and Haneke's searing vision is destined to haunt until our dying day.
reviews.author: Mattie Lucas

reviews.text: In a far more subtle fashion, Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva give an octogenarian master class in acting.
reviews.author: Brian D. Johnson

reviews.text: Amour is definitely a good film, but I'm judging this on the scale of Haneke's previous films where it just doesn't stand up.
reviews.author: C.J. Prince

reviews.text: This is a film that is hard to watch at times because of its realistic portrait of a couple in their final years, but it is one that should be seen. It's a love story that will stay with you long after you've left the theater.
reviews.author: Micheal Compton

reviews.text: Never easy but always tender, Amour is quietly unforgettable, and one of the best films of the year.
reviews.author: Molly Templeton

reviews.text: With Amour, Haneke has captured the grief of our own mortality in a delicate and profoundly humane way.
reviews.author: Patrick Gamble

reviews.text: Amour is indeed something special and very much worth the effort it takes to see it.
reviews.author: Kelly Jane Torrance

reviews.text: If only some of the uninhibitedly energetic thought and insight of these actors had found its way into Haneke's movie.
reviews.author: Richard Brody

reviews.text: Haneke has taken the ordinary - getting old; dying; happens to us all; no exceptions - and has transformed it into something so literate, powerful, terrifying, intelligent and extraordinary.
reviews.author: Deborah Ross

reviews.text: Lead performances makes it convincing to a point, but these poor characters are merely players in a signature act of desperation, Haneke style.
reviews.author: Pat Padua

reviews.text: Amour is a totally compelling, emotionally devastating movie, in which Haneke's technical trademarks support his overall theme.
reviews.author: Eve Tushnet

reviews.text: In our death-dreading Western culture, he deserves credit for unsentimentally and unflinchingly depicting the ugly realities of growing old and dealing with terminal illness.
reviews.author: Brandy McDonnell

reviews.text: What Haneke give us with Amour is a love story, one that is compassionate, powerful and intelligent, and that treats its protagonists and its audiences with respect.
reviews.author: Catherine Wheatley

reviews.text: [Director Michael Haneke] rarely moves the camera, and most of the film takes place inside an elderly couple's spacious apartment. Yet the film never seems claustrophobic.
reviews.author: Steve Erickson

reviews.text: It's undeniably tragic without being sentimental and easily the best non-American film of the year.
reviews.author: Kiko Martinez

reviews.text: Even for Haneke this is astringent stuff, light on visual flourish or narrative surprise, but driving it all are magnificent performances that cut right to the quick. The film's unblinking honesty has quiet integrity and power.
reviews.author: Lynden Barber

reviews.text: This movie has some heartbreaking moments and is moving, but on the lighter side, it is also somehow reassuring that we are never alone. Amour treats the subject of love in a manner that has seldom before been visited on screen.
reviews.author: Renuka Vyavahare

reviews.text: ... what distinguishes this carefully calculated Haneke ordeal from its previous incarnations is mostly the personal aspect: everyone is reminded of a death in his or her family.
reviews.author: Christoph Huber

reviews.text: What the film lacks in Haneke's usually impressive formal rigor, it makes up for with truly earned emotional truths.
reviews.author: Derek Smith

reviews.text: Although Amour deals with unquestionably somber topics, the film is accessible to anyone who has ever coped with a partner or parent's terminal illness.
reviews.author: Richard Porton

reviews.text: Scene after scene is an exquisite masterclass of astonishing acting.
reviews.author: Nick James

reviews.text: It's hard not to appreciate the film's extraordinary qualities. Jean-Louis Trintignant, Emmanuelle Riva, and Isabelle Huppert deliver performances so convincing and delicately nuanced that we forget they are actors, let alone French movie stars.
reviews.author: Francine Prose

reviews.text: I can't say you'll enjoy Amour. That would be an inappropriate reaction, in fact. Hollywood has conditioned us to expect swelling violins as characters draw close to death. (Here) there's little drama and nothing in the way of ceremony.
reviews.author: Bill Newcott

reviews.text: Beautifully shot, powerfully acted, and skillfully composed, Amour is worth pursuing.
reviews.author: Monica Castillo

reviews.text: Does what it sets out to do, expertly weaving together the monotony of everyday life, the nauseating horror of mortality, and the most esoteric corners of the human mind.
reviews.author: J. Olson

reviews.text: It's a chilling, pitiless vision that offers no relief, just a portrait of decline.
reviews.author: Sean Burns

reviews.text: Michael Haneke's profound new film Amour is far from your standard Hollywood romance. It is also a more nuanced, challenging and thought-provoking experience than that one word might lead you to believe.
reviews.author: T'Cha Dunlevy

reviews.text: Amour is a brutally difficult viewing experience, but it's in no way a film you'll desire -- or be able -- to forget.
reviews.author: Austin Trunick

reviews.text: The performances of Riva and Trintignant are revelatory.
reviews.author: Richard Knight

reviews.text: We wake from the best movies as witnesses; we feel the truth of what we have seen and heard, and though we know it's only a movie - just as we know in lucid dreams that we're actually asleep - we cannot help but feel changed by what we have seen.
reviews.author: Philip Martin

reviews.text: a profoundly humane and deeply challenging depiction of the emotional and physical ravages of old age
reviews.author: James Kendrick

reviews.text: Amour is a lesser work from Michael Haneke that features brilliant performances from Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva, but is held back by a simplistic narrative.
reviews.author: Jeff Beck

reviews.text: Compelling and incredibly heartbreaking...
reviews.author: Felix Vasquez Jr.

reviews.text: Michael Haneke gives us an unflinching look at love in the twilight years, placing a lot on the shoulders of two stars who come through like the veterans they are.
reviews.author: James Plath

reviews.text: Unnerving in its own way - heartfelt and tender, but with an undercurrent of foreboding.
reviews.author: Eric D. Snider

reviews.text: This is realism that enlarges our conception of the term.
reviews.author: Stanley Kauffmann

reviews.text: Now at the end of the year comes a masterpiece, not just the best of the year, but one of the best ever: Michael Haneke's Amour.
reviews.author: David Thomson

reviews.text: It leaves you spent, depressed and intensely afraid of the future. In some ways that's admirable, but like our fallible bodies, it gets old - fast.
reviews.author: Al Alexander

reviews.text: Haneke has created a gift for both audiences and the two legendary actors cast in the lead roles.
reviews.author: Matt Kelemen

reviews.text: In a film that's so explicitly cathartic for the filmmaker, there's a whole lotta catharsis withheld for the audience.
reviews.author: Sara Maria Vizcarrondo

reviews.text: While [director Michael] Haneke's love of long takes invite you to stare into the corrugated faces of Georges and Anne as their worlds change, there is a leaden quality to many stretches of the film that assume a profundity that simply isn't there.
reviews.author: Jim Schembri

reviews.text: Powerful piece of cinema that forces us to confront death and something even worse; the prospect of outliving the love of one's life
reviews.author: Cameron Williams

reviews.text: This beautifully-handled, deeply devastating work is all about the most human issue of all: we're all headed for the scrap-heap.
reviews.author: David 'Mad Dog' Bradley

reviews.text: Movingly acted and extremely harrowing.
reviews.author: Matt Glasby

reviews.text: Rarely has this subject matter been depicted so realistically, so honestly. You always know where the story is heading but it's still tough to watch.
reviews.author: Matthew Toomey

reviews.text: The scenario is upsetting, but the execution is genuine and pure, making Amour a film of heartbreaking beauty and Haneke's masterpiece.
reviews.author: Thomas Caldwell

reviews.text: Amour will now rate highly on a list of my favorite horror movies. It's certainly upsetting. But that is its strength.
reviews.author: Jeffrey Overstreet

reviews.text: This is a profound look at love about a couple who have lived with each other for so many years, know each other so well and this terrible thing that is facing them and there's a serenity there which makes it even more moving, I think.
reviews.author: David Stratton

reviews.text: It's Haneke's searing honesty and lack of sentimentality, and his talent as a writer-filmmaker that lifts this film to the heights of achievement. I know that the storyline may sound gloomy, the film is not. It is beyond wonderful.
reviews.author: Margaret Pomeranz

reviews.text: Ultimately, the title of the film demands to be taken as a question: is this truly what love looks like? A little smugly, Haneke refuses to answer.
reviews.author: Jake Wilson

reviews.text: A multiple award winner at film festivals around the globe, and it is easy to see why. Highly recommended.
reviews.author: Leigh Paatsch

reviews.text: Michael Haneke's most intimate and painfully truthful film - an exploration of what love means at the far end of life.
reviews.author: Simon Weaving

reviews.text: This is a movie almost too painful to watch at times, yet so masterfully composed and acted - Riva absolutely deserves her Oscar nomination, while Trintignant was robbed - that it's impossible to turn away.
reviews.author: Steve Persall

reviews.text: Georges' irreversible decision may be courageous, but it requires no sacrifice on the part of his creator: for Haneke, it's business as usual.
reviews.author: John Beifuss

reviews.text: Trintignant and Riva are unforgettably brilliant as the aging couple we can all identify with.
reviews.author: Dennis Schwartz

reviews.text: Haneke's startling film stands in stark contrast with other recent, comedic fare that seemingly addresses similar issues.
reviews.author: Ed Gibbs

reviews.text: My review is categorized as 'favourable' not because I enjoyed the film (that's not Michael Haneke's intent) but because I recognise what he is trying to say and that he says it with a unique cinematic voice
reviews.author: Andrew L. Urban

reviews.text: Debilitation and loss of control is a harsh topic, yet Haneke's film is surprisingly gentle, exploring the constraints and options faced, as old age delivers its ultimate blow - the loss of self and ability to function with dignity
reviews.author: Louise Keller

reviews.text: Amour is a pure depiction of love, in all its many forms.
reviews.author: Michael Smith

reviews.text: The furthest thing from sweet sorrow imaginable, Amour gets real about the pain of parting in every sense of the word.
reviews.author: Rick Kisonak

reviews.text: This subject matter is ripe for sentimentalization, but Haneke resists it at every turn, opting instead for unflinching honesty. It is the economy of theme paired with the subtle richness of character that make Amour so powerful.
reviews.author: Eric Melin

reviews.text: Clearly, Amour, Michael Haneke and Emmanuelle Riva don't really need me to additionally sing their praises (although praise is indeed all I have), so let's discuss Jean-Louis Trintignant for a moment.
reviews.author: Matt Brunson

reviews.text: Trintignant perfectly captures the resolve that eventually borders on obsession, as the woman he loves gradually, maddeningly, disappears before his eyes, and he does whatever he can to prevent it, though he knows it's impossible.
reviews.author: Bill Goodykoontz

reviews.text: All is presented in Haneke's exacting style, one that I find controlling and a bit, well, smothering.
reviews.author: Gary Thompson

reviews.text: An insightful, memorable film about what it means to love.
reviews.author: Marc Mohan

reviews.text: Many viewers will find echoes of their grandparents, parents, or even themselves in these characters.
reviews.author: James Berardinelli

reviews.text: A movie that is utterly worthy of its all-encompassing title.
reviews.author: Ann Hornaday

reviews.text: A tale about love at its most terribly, backbreakingly difficult.
reviews.author: Mark Deming

reviews.text: The resulting interplay of ruthless restraint and unavoidable passion, plus the film's refusal to shrink from depicting the inevitable horrors of physical deterioration, is devastating.
reviews.author: Kenneth Turan

reviews.text: In many ways, it's a horror film, as the woman descends into helplessness, and - like the audience - the man can only watch. It's a potent piece of filmmaking.
reviews.author: David Frese

reviews.text: The superb Trintignant and the Oscar-nominated Riva -- who would win, in a just world -- embody once-vigorous people in inevitable decline.
reviews.author: Lawrence Toppman

reviews.text: For Haneke, love is just another curious human trait to be dissected and used as a tool to disquiet his audience.
reviews.author: Josh Bell

reviews.text: A poignant tale of undying love!
reviews.author: Kam Williams

reviews.text: Beautifully acted and unflinching, Amour goes where few movies have the courage to
reviews.author: Robert Denerstein

reviews.text: Riva's performance is undeniably magnificent, as she must chart every step of Anne's physical and mental deteriorating with exacting precision.
reviews.author: Rob Thomas

reviews.text: In many ways it's the best horror film I've ever seen. At the same time, it's hard to recommend; I believe I will be struggling to forget this film as long as I live. I doubt I'll succeed.
reviews.author: Tom Long

reviews.text: Sadly effective, with two standout performances.
reviews.author: Rich Heldenfels

reviews.text: Death, illness and tragedy transcend demographics, and the characters in "Amour" are all of us in the end.
reviews.author: Duane Dudek

reviews.text: Moving, touching and beautifully acted. The question: Do audiences want to spend two hours watching an old couple go from sad to sadder to saddest?
reviews.author: Clint O'Connor

reviews.text: It is an inspirational film in the truest sense, and one to see with someone you love.
reviews.author: Calvin Wilson

reviews.text: ...this deceptively simple film makes clear that death, real death, the kind we all face and most art refuses to address honestly, is relentless and unsentimental.
reviews.author: Jeff Meyers

reviews.text: This is beautiful film, and a terrible one: devastating to stick out, and yet one of the most remarkable romances ever made...
reviews.author: MaryAnn Johanson

reviews.text: As remarkable as Haneke's films are, not a one has been as transcendently generous as Amour, which is nominated for five Academy Awards, including best picture, best director and best foreign-language film.
reviews.author: Lisa Kennedy

reviews.text: Death is part of love's bargain, and Haneke lays this fact bare.
reviews.author: Marjorie Baumgarten

reviews.text: It is hard to recommend Amour. Austrian director Michael Haneke's film cannot justly be described as entertaining, and it will likely leave you sad and weary. But it is a film you must see.
reviews.author: Matthew Odam

reviews.text: "Amour" isn't easy to watch, but its rewards are many.
reviews.author: Moira MacDonald

reviews.text: "Amour" isn't just a great movie, it's a movie that may actually do you some good.
reviews.author: Rafer Guzman

reviews.text: "Amour" isn't a fun time out at the movies, and I kind of doubt I'll ever see it again. But it's an amazingly act, absolutely heartbreaking film.
reviews.author: Stephen Silver

reviews.text: Shot in long, static takes, Amour stares directly into the indignities of old age and the curse of a slow death.
reviews.author: Rene Rodriguez

reviews.text: This is a masterpiece.
reviews.author: Steven Rea

reviews.text: Relativamente doce para os padrões de um cineasta acostumado a torturar seu público e a encarar a humanidade com imenso ceticismo, representa uma experiência difícil por nos lembrar o tempo inteiro de que todos dividiremos o mesmo desfecho.
reviews.author: Pablo Villaça

reviews.text: A bitter, pitiless piece of work. We can admire its components, but we're repulsed by its vision.
reviews.author: Kelly Vance

reviews.text: Haneke's self-indulgent approach is getting old to me. His devoted fans will like it, but others will most likely be scratching their heads trying to figure out how this got a Best Picture nomination.
reviews.author: Austin Kennedy

reviews.text: It's upsetting material lined with lead by Haneke, who searches for the meaning of love but can't help but dwell on the details of decay.
reviews.author: Brian Orndorf

reviews.text: There's nowhere to hide: The film cuts no corners and stings with the authenticity of life's fragility.
reviews.author: Chris Vognar

reviews.text: The movie avoids melodrama; instead, it's just extraordinarily intimate, with touches of visual poetry like the pigeon that gets into the apartment and won't leave, an image of our own heedless tenacity.
reviews.author: Ty Burr

reviews.text: Amour is as heartbreaking and real as it gets.
reviews.author: Mark Sells

reviews.text: Tough and beautiful, it secures Haneke's reputation as one of the world's best.
reviews.author: Chris Hewitt

reviews.text: Two of the world's best actors, Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva, play Amour's octogenarian couple, so it's surprising that the characters aren't very interesting.
reviews.author: Peter Keough

reviews.text: Haneke addresses the ravaging effects of aging in a starkly intimate way but Amour oddly lacks affectivity. Something that should be overflowing with emotion is strangely as sterile as Georges and Anne's Parisian apartment.
reviews.author: Erick Weber

reviews.text: unforgettable portrait of old age
reviews.author: John A. Nesbit

reviews.text: The audacious performances by both veteran actors are wonderful, and the film never resorts to cheap sentimentality.
reviews.author: Todd Jorgenson

reviews.text: Powerful and well-acted, this drama meticulously captures the pain and perils of aging in a way that will be hard to forget.
reviews.author: John Hanlon

reviews.text: Haneke treats Georges and Anne with absolute respect, never pandering to sentiment or cliché and most assuredly not sugarcoating the experience of walking one's partner through suffering, toward death.
reviews.author: Alison Gang

reviews.text: Haneke doesn't offer easy solutions or pat emotions. He merely offers us a chance to eavesdrop and holds a mirror up to our own fears of old age, hopes for love, and challenges through life.
reviews.author: Brian Tallerico

reviews.text: The film is a graphic portrayal of the unfunny end game we're all fated to play; the title is just a simple declaration of how best to play it.
reviews.author: Rick Groen

reviews.text: A confident, lovingly articulated mood piece about a subject that is universal, yet rarely told.
reviews.author: Dustin Putman

reviews.text: "Amour" is also unforgettable and one of a kind, two hours of torment that, in the end, you will probably not regret.
reviews.author: Mick LaSalle

reviews.text: Small, sure and stunningly acted, this is a picture of exacting control, which is to be expected from Haneke, whose works include Cache and The White Ribbon.
reviews.author: Michael Phillips

reviews.text: [Haneke] has put his finger on a very particular kind of heartbreak: seeing a lover give up not on you but on the life you've shared.
reviews.author: J. R. Jones

reviews.text: A masterpiece of restraint, intelligence and humanity.
reviews.author: Bruce Kirkland

reviews.text: Amour is the simplest yet most passionate film of Haneke's incredible career.
As it unflinchingly faces mortality, Amour is full of incomparably beautiful and sad moments.
reviews.author: Claudia Puig

reviews.text: Often looks and hurts like seeing real lives in real time. Is that enough? Honesty gradually becomes simplicity as the film's reality outweighs its insight.
reviews.author: Matt Pais

reviews.text: The most brutally honest picture ever made about growing old and wasting away.
reviews.author: A.A. Dowd

reviews.text: Old age isn't for sissies, and neither is this film.
reviews.author: Roger Ebert

reviews.text: A wrenching film that is sure to bring tears -- a lot of tears -- to your eyes and manages, in many ways, to affirm that love is worth sharing and life is worth living even in the most final of days.
reviews.author: Charlie McCollum

reviews.text: The story is heart-breaking in its honest depiction of life near the end.
reviews.author: Robin Clifford

reviews.text: The film has been declared a masterpiece by many, and yet the director's inability to put aside his usual chilly remove encases "Amour's" protagonists under glass.
reviews.author: Laura Clifford

reviews.text: There have been many invasions in Haneke's work, and there is indeed an attempted break-in at the start of this film, but nothing compares with the looming approach of mortality.
reviews.author: Anthony Lane

reviews.text: Haneke, a master of icy appraisal, here contemplates an elderly Parisian couple at the very end of their lives.
reviews.author: Kurt Loder

reviews.text: An examination of life and death, this minimalist film succeeds on all levels.
reviews.author: Ron Wilkinson

reviews.text: On paper it's a welcome change of pace for Haneke, but his tendency to treat the couple as patients rather than characters -- at a cold remove rather than with a warm embrace -- feels at odds with the material.
reviews.author: Michael Nordine

reviews.text: The film's power stems from the way Haneke avoids milking the viewer's sympathy.
reviews.author: Ethan Alter

reviews.text: Intimate, admirable and elegant, it's, nevertheless, demanding, deliberate and depressing - about facing our own mortality.
reviews.author: Susan Granger

reviews.text: It is a stunning film.
reviews.author: David Edelstein

reviews.text: A film so honest in dealing with end-of-life issues that its purity is a positive rebuke to all the maudlin movies on the subject.
reviews.author: Frank Swietek

reviews.text: Michael Haneke wants to remind us all that we are going to die someday, and that the long day's journey into night is probably not going to be a pleasant one
reviews.author: Kurt Halfyard

reviews.text: Amour might seem hardly the stuff of entertainment, yet the reason it has been acclaimed isn't mysterious. Confronting death, it studies life, closely and lovingly.
reviews.author: Joe Morgenstern

reviews.text: Because of its subject matter, and because of the actors, it's impossible to watch this film without being moved. But a martinet is running the show.
reviews.author: Peter Rainer

reviews.text: A compassionate, rigorously unsentimental masterwork from a director who doesn't normally truck in emotions like the one named in the title.
reviews.author: Dana Stevens

reviews.text: This is an unforgettable love story set at the close of day, as tragic and beautiful in its way as "Tristan und Isolde," and a portrait of the impossible beauty and fragility of life that will yield new experiences to every viewer and every viewing.
reviews.author: Andrew O'Hehir

reviews.text: Gains its power from grounding its characters' pain in something humanistic.
reviews.author: Tim Brayton

reviews.text: Profoundly moving, unflinchingly honest and tender with brave, emotionally raw performances by Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva.
reviews.author: Avi Offer

reviews.text: Mundanely horrifying and extremely powerful.
reviews.author: Jonah Flicker

reviews.text: A relentless and shattering masterwork, 'Amour' breaks the heart but satisfies the soul.
reviews.author: Kathleen Murphy

reviews.text: All great films have imagination; this one also has the sense of experience.
reviews.author: Farran Smith Nehme

reviews.text: The story behind the central tableau ... starts off completely mundane, shifts into a tale of pain and sadness, and ends on a note of horror mixed with tortured understanding.
reviews.author: Mark Dujsik

reviews.text: If Haneke has any real interest in keeping art cinema alive, he should take some notes from the Queensbridge rapper Nas.
reviews.author: Radheyan Simonpillai

reviews.text: Growing old is a war, and movies rarely go there. Michael Haneke's amazing, dignified "Amour" is the exception.
reviews.author: Joe Neumaier

reviews.text: In the history of movies about love, Amour shall last forever.
reviews.author: Mary Corliss

reviews.text: If you've seen someone you love through their dying, it may burn you up - but in an illuminating way.
reviews.author: Ella Taylor

reviews.text: Haneke remains, by his rules, infallible. So what?
reviews.author: Nick Pinkerton

reviews.text: I am glad I saw it -- and hope I never see it again.
reviews.author: Matt Singer

reviews.text: Haneke being Haneke, Amour is still a bracingly unsentimental film, but it shouldn't be mistaken for heartless.
reviews.author: Scott Tobias

reviews.text: ...true to the awfulness of aging, yet Haneke also unveils a trait I didn't previously associate with him: mercy.
reviews.author: Josh Larsen

reviews.text: While this might not be the post-gift-unwrapping movie destination of choice this holiday season, the brutal honesty and emotional truth of Amour make it one of this year's best films.
reviews.author: Alonso Duralde

reviews.text: It's an uncompromising portrait of the aging process, with the experience of getting older rendered in a harsh light rather than a comforting golden glow.
reviews.author: Robert Levin

reviews.text: It will surely strike a chord with anyone who's watched a loved one slip away in this manner, whether it's a parent or a spouse.
reviews.author: Christy Lemire

reviews.text: Consummate acting helps ease a painful watch, as Michael Haneke describes the ultimate test of love in a profoundly honest study of sickness and dying.
reviews.author: Deborah Young

reviews.text: Achieves an emotional level that probably would dismay the dispassionate Haneke. It's a hard film to recommend, because it will hit too close to home for a lot of people.
reviews.author: Marshall Fine

reviews.text: art-house fans who do venture forth into the grim but incredibly poignant  Amour  will be richly rewarded.
reviews.author: Doris Toumarkine

reviews.text: The title is french for love. The movie itself, indisputably the year's best foreign-language film and an Oscar front-runner, defines what love is. And it does it the hard way.
reviews.author: Peter Travers

reviews.text: It is, more than any of Haneke's previous work, infused with compassion, but of a sort that cuts like a knife.
reviews.author: Alison Willmore

reviews.text: Amour is not an easy film by any stretch of the imagination, but for those in search of art without pretension or affectation, this is the way it's done.
reviews.author: Joshua Starnes

reviews.text: Both a poignant love story and a typically rigorous attempt to dismantle one of the last great taboos in cinema.
reviews.author: Michael Bonner

reviews.text: I urge you to share its sweetness and wisdom, and learn something.
reviews.author: Rex Reed

reviews.text: Haneke's challenge to audiences is to experience real love - it's tough and brutal and definitely not for the faint of heart.
reviews.author: Kirk Honeycutt

reviews.text: A devastating movie with some of the finest acting you're ever likely to see. But- it's very grim. Makes AWAY FROM HER look like AIRPLANE.
reviews.author: Chris Bumbray

reviews.text: Without doubt, this is one of the films of the year that everyone should see.
reviews.author: Graham Young

reviews.text: Severely tests the marriage vow "...in sickness and in health..."
reviews.author: Harvey S. Karten

reviews.text: Amour broke my heart and lifted my soul. This is a unique film about the death of love, not a doomed romance but the inevitable end to a lifelong passionate relationship.
reviews.author: Brian Henry Martin

reviews.text: Haneke's undeniably austere film doesn't offer any false consolation, but it remains tender and compassionate, and boasts brave, heart-rending performances from a pair of French screen icons.
reviews.author: Jason Best

reviews.text: Michael Haneke's effortlessly graceful picture will come to be seen as one of the greatest films about the confrontation of death and ageing.
reviews.author: Philip French

reviews.text: A striking look at a long-term relationship, this film is an antidote to those who are tired of shamelessly sweet depictions of retirees, such as The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel or Hope Springs.
reviews.author: Rich Cline

reviews.text: It is unequivocally a masterpiece.
reviews.author: David Sexton

reviews.text: From the first moment to the very last, you'll be convinced Georges and Anne are true soulmates.
reviews.author: Grant Rollings

reviews.text: It is beautifully acted by leads Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva and inspires sympathy.
reviews.author: Henry Fitzherbert

reviews.text: The film is pitiless, mordant, touching, humane - so where dwells the horror? In the plot that lies beneath: the life-or-death siege, spooky, implacable and remorseless.
reviews.author: Nigel Andrews

reviews.text: Haneke's lesser films can have a finger-wagging quality and this does not: it modulates from tonal disquiet to a profound and moving calm - towards silence, in fact.
reviews.author: Tim Robey

reviews.text: There's no empathy here and no genuine insight either.
reviews.author: Alistair Harkness

reviews.text: The performances of the two astonishing French actors in Amour makes this a gripping and possibly provocative drama.
reviews.author: Siobhan Synnot

reviews.text: Haneke has now created a film that hits you in the gut, and elicits a deeper emotional response than any of his features have in the past.
reviews.author: Philip Concannon

reviews.text: A haunting and emotionally devastating drama with a strong script and a pair of powerhouse performances from veteran actors Jean-Louis Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva.
reviews.author: Matthew Turner

reviews.text: Dignified and humane, it's Haneke's most touching piece...and perhaps his best movie.
reviews.author: Tim Evans

reviews.text: Old age may not be a reality you wish to confront, but you must see this film.
reviews.author: David Hughes

reviews.text: Far from being a cold, scientific study from a filmmaker frequently accused of placing a pane of glass between his work and his viewers, this sensitive film emerges heartfelt and humane.
reviews.author: Jamie Graham

reviews.text: Haneke's film is unquestionably the feel-bad film of the year, refreshingly lacking in sentiment and absolutely devastating, but also abuzz with the joys that make life worth living.
reviews.author: Shaun Munro

reviews.text: Thoughtful and unsentimental, though not unfeeling. A stunning, near-perfect movie.
reviews.author: Fr. Chris Carpenter

reviews.text: A masterpiece.
reviews.author: Craig Skinner

reviews.text: Haneke goes far beyond pushing emotional buttons into territory where our most visceral fears lurk.
reviews.author: Amber Wilkinson

reviews.text: Michael Haneke's elegiac exploration of an elderly couple's final days together transcends all definition of romantic ideal.
reviews.author: Cole Smithey

reviews.text: Haneke ... knows the reality of growing old together isn't for the faint of heart.
reviews.author: Stephanie Zacharek

reviews.text: This isn't the work of a newly moral or humanistic filmmaker, but another ruse by the same unscrupulous showman whose funny games have been beguiling us for years.
reviews.author: Calum Marsh

reviews.text: A poignant and provocative French-language drama about the tenderness, discipline, and patience involved in being a loving caregiver.
reviews.author: Frederic and Mary Ann Brussat

reviews.text: Life is full of unfair horrors; that is why we go to the cinema. Amour is the cinematic equivalent of telling a child Santa doesn't exist.
reviews.author: Adam Ross

reviews.text: The type of metaphysical mediation on marriage, love, and death that insists, allows, and rewards introspection.
reviews.author: Sam Fragoso

reviews.text: ...the movie, which rarely leaves the couple's apartment, adopts a palpably repetitive feel that slowly-but-surely drains the viewer's interest...
reviews.author: David Nusair

reviews.text: Leaves you feeling as if you watched a solid character drama with above-average performances, but it doesn't stand up to some of Haneke's more daring films.
reviews.author: Edward Douglas

reviews.text: The unflinching "Amour" captures a loving couple's last days with documentary-worthy realism, nailing the frustrations, struggles and small joys that often come with the caretaking of a loved one.
reviews.author: Sean O'Connell

reviews.text: Haneke communicates all the minutia and indignity of a slow and inevitable death.
reviews.author: Tom Clift

reviews.text: A two-hour portrait of human existence at its most fucking-hell-when-will-it-end brutal.
reviews.author: Charlie Lyne

reviews.text: If we were previously in any doubt, Haneke is confirmed as the premiere European director of his generation.
reviews.author: Donald Clarke

reviews.text: Amour is harrowing, emotional, thrilling, intense, beautiful, tragic, and powerful cinema.
reviews.author: Blake Howard

reviews.text: Haneke plays no funny games on the audience in his considerate and humanistic Amour, though it will have you begging for a remote control all the same; to wind back the clock and return to better times between Georges and Anne.
reviews.author: Simon Miraudo

reviews.text: A sober, gorgeously directed portrait of an elderly couple facing terrifying questions of life and death.
reviews.author: Jon Frosch

reviews.text: It is uncomfortable, unrelenting and in turn undeniably powerful.
reviews.author: Gail Tolley

reviews.text: It's a universal tale that is at times touching and horrifying and always powerful.
reviews.author: Kaleem Aftab

reviews.text: Beautifully and bravely acted, Amour is an unflinching depiction of the daily toll that old-age degeneration exacts upon its victims. Should be required viewing for anyone intending to grow old.
reviews.author: Kimberly Gadette

reviews.text: A tender, wrenching, impeccably directed story of love and death.
reviews.author: Manohla Dargis

reviews.text: Haneke maintains a degree of ambiguity about the outcomes. He might get a bad rap for his apparent obsession with human suffering, but this investigation of it from dual-perspectives couldn't be made by anyone else.
reviews.author: Fiona Williams

reviews.text: Haneke trains his merciless rigor-leavened, for perhaps the first time ever, with deeply felt tenderness and compassion-on the most universally heartbreaking aspect of the human condition: old age and its myriad indignities.
reviews.author: Mike D'Angelo

reviews.text: Clear-eyed, cool-headed and profoundly humane, Love is the consummate anti-weepie.
reviews.author: Robbie Collin

reviews.text: Transfixing and extraordinarily touching, perhaps the most hauntingly honest movie about old age ever made
reviews.author: Owen Gleiberman

reviews.text: Hanekes absolute control makes the film intensely involving and quietly moving, rather than harrowing.
reviews.author: Jonathan Romney

reviews.text: Haneke is the first Competition film director at Cannes this year to both succeed totally on the terms he sets out for himself, and truly challenge the audience to bear witness to something they've never seen on screen before.
reviews.author: Karina Longworth

reviews.text: Amour has no substance, no style, no joy, no passion, no flavor at all. It's just quiet scenes one after another, presented in a way that will connect with some, but not all.
reviews.author: Alex Billington

reviews.text: Infused with its namesake, this gentle tragedy is the filmmaker's least complicated work to date, a streamlined tearjerker that respects viewers enough to not jerk the tears out of them.
reviews.author: David Fear

reviews.text: An exceptional work shows a world-class director still unafraid to lock horns with the profound mysteries of the universe.
reviews.author: David Jenkins

reviews.text: Considering Haneke's confrontational past, this poignantly acted, uncommonly tender two-hander makes a doubly powerful statement about man's capacity for dignity and sensitivity when confronted with the inevitable cruelty of nature.
reviews.author: Peter Debruge

reviews.text: 'Amour' is a devastating, highly intelligent and astonishingly performed work. It's a masterpiece.
reviews.author: Dave Calhoun

reviews.text: Michael Haneke's new film in the Cannes competition is everything that could have been expected from him and more: a moving, terrifying and uncompromising drama of extraordinary intimacy and intelligence.
reviews.author: Peter Bradshaw

reviews.text: Intensely intimate drama for two sharply observed characters, superlatively played by Trintignant and Emmanuelle Riva, Haneke's Love contests personal and societal definitions of love, marriage, aging, illnes, and dying.
reviews.author: Emanuel Levy

synopsis: Retired music teachers Georges (Jean-Louis Trintignant) and Anne (Emmanuelle Riva) have spent their lives devoted to their careers and to each other. Their relationship faces its greatest challenge when Anne suffers a debilitating stroke. Though Georges himself suffers from the aches and infirmities of old age, he bravely ignores his own discomfort to take care of his wife, and is determined to keep his promise to her that she never go back to the hospital.
